questions.prompt: Which forms of specialization are available for a function template?
options: Both full and partial specialization, exactly as for a class template.
Partial specialization only; full specialization is spelled as an overload.
Full specialization only; for partial behaviour you write an overload instead.
Neither; a function template can only be overloaded or constrained.
questions.explanation: Function templates may be fully specialized (`template <> void f<int>(int)`) but never partially — that asymmetry is the whole reason `template <class T> void f(T*)` is an overload rather than a specialization. The 'both, exactly as for a class template' option is the tempting one because class templates really do support both; function templates instead lean on overloading plus partial ordering.

questions.prompt: Given `template <class T> void f(T);` (1), `template <class T> void f(T*);` (2), and `template <> void f<int>(int);` (3), what happens for `int* p; f(p);`?
options: (2) is selected by overload resolution; the specialization (3) is never even considered.
(3) is selected, because an explicit specialization outranks any template overload.
(1) is selected, because having a specialization makes it the more specialized candidate.
The call is ambiguous between the pointer overload and the `int` specialization.
questions.explanation: Overload resolution runs over the primary templates only; partial ordering picks (2) as more specialized for a pointer argument. The 'a specialization outranks an overload' option is the classic misconception Sutter warns about: specializations do not participate in overload resolution at all — the compiler picks a primary first, then looks for a specialization of that one, and (3) specializes (1), not (2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about alias templates is true?
options: They admit full specialization but not partial, matching the rule for function templates.
They introduce a distinct type, so an alias can add a new overload for the aliased type.
They admit partial specialization, which is how `type_identity_t` blocks deduction.
They admit no specialization at all, and are transparent: the alias and the aliased type are one type.
questions.explanation: An alias template is not a class: it has neither full nor partial specialization, and `Vec<int>` *is* `std::vector<int, MyAlloc<int>>`, so it cannot create a distinct type to overload on. The `type_identity_t` option is the seductive one — that idiom works because a qualified nested name is a non-deduced context, not because anything is partially specialized.

questions.prompt: With `int a[5];`, `template <class T> void byval(T);` and `template <class T> void byref(T&);`, what does each call deduce?
options: Both deduce `T = int*`, because array-to-pointer decay is applied before deduction in every case.
`byval` deduces `T = int*`; `byref` deduces `T = int[5]`, since decay applies only to by-value parameters.
Both deduce `T = int[5]`, because deduction is a pattern match that never applies any adjustment.
`byval` deduces `T = int[5]`; `byref` deduces `T = int*`, since binding a reference forces the decay.
questions.explanation: For a by-value parameter the compiler drops top-level cv and applies array/function decay before matching; for a reference parameter neither adjustment happens, so the extent survives. That preservation is exactly what makes `template <class T, size_t N> void arr(T(&)[N])` capture `N = 5`. The 'decay always happens' option confuses the by-value rule for a universal one, and the reversed option has the direction backwards.

questions.prompt: Why does `template <class T> T max(T, T); max(1, 2.0);` fail to compile?
options: Because the arguments differ in value category, so no consistent `T&&` collapsing exists.
Because `T` deduces to `int` from one argument and `double` from the other, and deduction applies no arithmetic conversions.
Because deduction takes only the first argument's type, so the `double` argument is rejected as narrowing.
Because the return type `T` is ambiguous, though the parameters themselves deduce consistently.
questions.explanation: Deduction is a pattern match: only decay, qualification conversion, and derived-to-`Base<T>` are permitted, so no integral promotion or arithmetic conversion can reconcile `int` with `double`. Writing `max<double>(1, 2.0)` fixes it because supplying `T` explicitly skips deduction and lets ordinary implicit conversions run. The 'first argument wins' option describes nothing the language does — all deductions for one parameter must agree exactly.

questions.prompt: Which parameter is a forwarding reference?
options: Exactly `T&&` where `T` is being deduced by this call, plus `auto&&`.
Any rvalue-reference parameter inside a template, including `const T&&` and `std::vector<T>&&`.
Any `T&&`, including `void m(T&&)` on a member of an already-instantiated class template.
Any parameter written with `&&`, plus any `const auto&` parameter of a generic lambda.
questions.explanation: The form must be the bare `T&&` with `T` deduced by that very call, or `auto&&` — nothing else. The member-function option is the one that catches people: inside `template <class T> struct S { void m(T&& x); }` the parameter `T` was already fixed when the class was instantiated, so `m` takes a plain rvalue reference and does no deduction. `const T&&` and `std::vector<T>&&` fail the 'bare form' test.

questions.prompt: `struct Widget { template <class T> Widget(T&&); Widget(const Widget&); };` and `Widget w1{"x"}; Widget w2{w1};` — which constructor runs for `w2`?
options: The copy constructor: a non-template candidate always beats a template candidate regardless of match quality.
The template: `w1` is a non-const lvalue, so `T = Widget&` is an exact match while the copy ctor must add const.
The copy constructor: a constructor template is never a candidate for constructing from its own class type.
Neither — the call is ambiguous, because both candidates are exact matches on a non-const lvalue.
questions.explanation: Forwarding references are greedy: binding `Widget&` to a non-const lvalue is an identity match, whereas the copy constructor needs a qualification conversion to `const Widget&`, so the template wins and the 'copy' silently isn't one. The non-template tiebreaker option states a real rule backwards in scope — non-templates win only when the two candidates are *equally good*, and here they are not. Fix it with `requires (!std::derived_from<std::remove_cvref_t<T>, Widget>)`.

questions.prompt: For `template <class T> void f(T&& x); int i = 0; f(i); f(42);` what are `T` and the parameter type in each call?
options: `f(i)`: `T = int&`, parameter `int&&`, because `& &&` collapses to `&&`.
`f(i)`: `T = int`, parameter `int&&`; `f(42)`: `T = int&&`, parameter `int&&`.
Both give `T = int` and parameter `int&&`; the caller's value category is recovered later by `std::forward`.
`f(i)`: `T = int&`, parameter `int&`; `f(42)`: `T = int`, parameter `int&&`.
questions.explanation: The special rule for `T&&` deduces `T = A&` from an lvalue and `T = A` from an rvalue; collapsing then turns `int& &&` into `int&`. The option claiming `& &&` collapses to `&&` inverts the table — lvalue reference is infectious, so any `&` in the pair wins and only `&& &&` yields `&&`. Note that in *both* cases the named parameter `x` is itself an lvalue, which is precisely why `std::forward` is needed.

questions.prompt: `std::vector<int> v2{1,2,3}; std::vector v{v2};` — what is `v`?
options: A `std::vector<int>` that is a copy of `v2`, because the copy-deduction candidate wins.
A `std::vector<std::vector<int>>` holding one element, since the initializer-list candidate matches exactly.
Ill-formed, because CTAD cannot choose between copying `v2` and wrapping it in a new vector.
A `std::vector<int>` of size 3 default-initialized, via the count constructor taking `v2.size()`.
questions.explanation: CTAD's candidate set always includes a copy-deduction candidate, and for a single argument of the same class template it beats the initializer-list candidate — so you get a copy, not a nested vector. The 'nested vector' answer is what most people expect and is the whole reason this is a famous pitfall; `std::pair p{p2}` behaves the same way. Nothing here is ambiguous, so the ill-formed option is wrong too.

questions.prompt: What happens with `std::pair<int> p{1, 2.0};`?
options: It deduces the second argument as `double`, since CTAD fills in any omitted trailing arguments.
It is ill-formed, because deduction guides may not be used when any argument is written explicitly.
It is ill-formed, because CTAD is all-or-nothing and never completes a partial argument list.
It deduces the second argument as `int`, since the written argument constrains both parameters.
questions.explanation: CTAD applies only when the template-argument list is entirely absent; a partial list like `std::pair<int>` disables it and simply leaves the class under-specified. The 'fills in the rest' option is the natural guess by analogy with function templates, where you really can supply some arguments explicitly and deduce the remainder — that flexibility exists for function templates, not for CTAD. The other ill-formed option gives a rule that does not exist.

questions.prompt: What did C++20 add to the set of permitted non-type template parameter types?
options: Structural class types and floating point, which is what enables string literals as template arguments.
Any literal class type, including ones with private members or a user-provided copy constructor.
`std::string` and `std::vector`, because their member functions became `constexpr`.
Floating point only; class types remain forbidden, so string literals still need `auto` NTTPs.
questions.explanation: C++20 admits *structural* types — literal class types whose members are all public, non-mutable and themselves structural, with no user-provided copy/move/destructor — plus floating point. That is what lets a `FixedString` wrapper carry a string literal as a template argument. The 'any literal class type' option is the near-miss: private members and a user-provided copy constructor both disqualify a type, and `std::string` fails on top of that because it allocates.

questions.prompt: A C++20 structural type defines a `constexpr operator==` that reports two objects with different member values as equal. Are `X<a>` and `X<b>` the same type for those two values?
options: Yes — the compiler invokes the type's `constexpr operator==` to decide template-argument equivalence.
No — two NTTP arguments of class type are never equivalent, so every use yields a fresh distinct type.
Yes — any two arguments of one structural type collapse to a single instantiation whatever their values.
No — template-argument equivalence for structural types is member-wise, so `operator==` has no say.
questions.explanation: Identity of instantiations is decided by member-wise template-argument equivalence, deliberately bypassing any user-defined comparison — a class does not get to redefine what makes two template arguments the same. The `operator==` option is tempting because the type is otherwise fully constexpr-usable, but overload resolution never enters this decision. Equivalent arguments genuinely do collapse to one type; it is the *criterion*, not the collapsing, that the wrong answers get wrong.

questions.prompt: Which row of the specialization table is stated correctly?
options: Variable templates support full specialization only, matching the rule for function templates.
Alias templates support partial specialization only, which is how the `_t` trait aliases are written.
Class templates support partial specialization only; fully specializing a class template is ill-formed.
Variable templates support both full and partial specialization since C++14; alias templates support neither.
questions.explanation: Variable templates got both kinds of specialization in C++14 — that is exactly how the one-line `is_same_v` is written, with `template <class T> inline constexpr bool is_same_v<T, T> = true;`. Alias templates support neither. The class-template option is the sharpest distractor because partial specialization is what class templates are famous for, but full specialization (`template <> struct Pair<int,int>`) is equally legal.

questions.prompt: One TU includes a header that instantiates `std::hash<Key>` before a full specialization of it is declared; another TU sees the specialization first. What is the status of the program?
options: IFNDR: the two TUs silently get different behaviour and no diagnostic is required.
A hard compile error in whichever TU instantiated the primary before seeing the specialization.
Well-formed: the specialization retroactively replaces the earlier instantiation within that TU.
A link error, since the two TUs emit COMDAT symbols with the same name but different bodies.
questions.explanation: A full specialization must be visible before the first use that would instantiate the primary, in *every* TU; violating that is ill-formed, no diagnostic required. The link-error answer is the most plausible wrong one because differing COMDAT bodies really do exist here — but the linker's job is to fold same-named weak symbols, not to compare them, so it happily keeps whichever it sees first and the bug ships silently.

questions.prompt: `template <class T> struct Holder { T v; void print() { std::cout << v; } };` and `Holder<NoStream> h;` where `NoStream` has no `operator<<`. What happens?
options: It fails: instantiating the class instantiates the definitions of all its member functions, `print` included.
It fails: `std::cout` in `print` is a non-dependent name bound and checked at the point of definition.
It compiles: `print`'s body is instantiated only if `print` is called, so nothing checks `operator<<` yet.
It compiles, but only because in-class definitions are implicitly inline and inline bodies are never checked.
questions.explanation: Member functions of a class template are instantiated lazily, on use — which is why `std::vector<T>` works for a `T` without a default constructor until you call `resize(n)`. The `std::cout` option is the trap worth dissecting: the name `std::cout` really is non-dependent and really is bound in phase one, but the *expression* `std::cout << v` depends on `T`, so its validity is deferred; binding a name is not the same as type-checking the expression containing it. Virtual members are the genuine exception, since the vtable forces them.

questions.prompt: Which members of a class template are instantiated as soon as the class itself is instantiated?
options: Constructors and the destructor, since the compiler must fix the object's initialization cost.
Virtual member functions, because the vtable has to be emitted; the rest wait until they are used.
Every member defined inside the class body, since in-class definitions are implicitly inline.
None at all — even virtual members wait until a call through a base pointer needs the vtable.
questions.explanation: Virtuals are the exception to lazy member instantiation: the vtable must be emitted with the class, so every virtual is instantiated whether or not it is called. The 'none at all' option sounds like a stricter version of the correct laziness rule, but it cannot hold — the vtable is a single object emitted at class instantiation and cannot be deferred per call site. Constructors and destructors follow the ordinary lazy rule like any other non-virtual member.

questions.prompt: `void g(double); template <class T> void f(T t) { g(t); } void g(int); f(1);` — which `g` is called?
options: `g(int)`: the dependent call `g(t)` is looked up entirely at the point of instantiation, where `g(int)` is visible.
`g(int)`: overload resolution runs at instantiation and prefers the exact match over the conversion.
Ill-formed: a dependent call resolves only through ADL, and ADL on an `int` argument finds no candidates.
`g(double)`: ordinary lookup for a dependent call happens at the definition point, and ADL on `int` adds nothing.
questions.explanation: Phase two adds only *ADL* at the point of instantiation; ordinary unqualified lookup is not redone there, so the later-declared `g(int)` is invisible and the `int` converts to `double`. The two `g(int)` options both assume plain lookup is repeated at instantiation, which is the single most common misreading of two-phase lookup. The call is not ill-formed either — the definition-point candidate `g(double)` is viable, which is exactly why customization points must be ADL-reachable.

questions.prompt: A template body contains a construct that is ill-formed and does not depend on any template parameter. The template is never instantiated anywhere in the program. What does a conforming compiler do?
options: Diagnoses it: non-dependent constructs are checked in phase one, at the point of definition.
Accepts it: nothing inside a template body is checked until an instantiation is requested.
Diagnoses it only if the enclosing header is included by more than one translation unit.
Warns in phase one and escalates to an error only if the template is later instantiated.
questions.explanation: Phase one checks syntax and type-checks every non-dependent construct at the point of definition, so an error there fires even for a template nobody uses. The 'nothing is checked until instantiation' answer describes MSVC's historical non-conforming behaviour, which is why `/permissive-` exists and why code can compile on Windows only. This is also why `static_assert(false)` in an untaken `if constexpr` branch used to fire — it was non-dependent, until CWG2518 carved out an exception.

questions.prompt: `template <class T> struct Derived : Base<T> { void f() { value = 1; } };` where `Base<T>` has an `int value`. What happens, and why?
options: It compiles on GCC and Clang but fails on MSVC, which is what `/permissive-` was added to fix.
It compiles: the base is instantiated first, so its members are visible to unqualified lookup in the derived class.
It fails: `value` needs a `typename` disambiguator, since a member of a dependent base is assumed to be a type.
It fails: unqualified lookup does not enter a dependent base, so `this->value` or a using-declaration is required.
questions.explanation: `Base<T>` is dependent, and some specialization of it might not have `value` at all, so phase-one unqualified lookup skips it entirely; `this->value`, `Base<T>::value`, or `using Base<T>::value;` all make the name dependent and defer it to instantiation. The MSVC option has the platforms exactly backwards — this is the archetypal 'works on MSVC, fails on GCC/Clang' bug. `typename` is for dependent *type* names, not for data members.

questions.prompt: A header declares `extern template class RingBuffer<Order>;` and one `.cpp` provides the explicit instantiation definition. What is the trade-off?
options: Compile time and object size improve, but the definition is no longer visible for inlining unless LTO is on.
Compile time improves with no effect on inlining, since the definition is still visible in the header.
Runtime improves, because the single shared instantiation stays resident in the instruction cache.
Object size improves but compile time worsens, since every TU must still parse and instantiate the class.
questions.explanation: `extern template` suppresses implicit instantiation in every other TU, so the compiler does the work once instead of N times and the linker has no duplicates to discard — but the call sites now see only a declaration, so the body cannot be inlined without link-time optimization. The 'inlining is unaffected' option is the trap: the template *definition* text is still in the header, yet the whole point of the declaration is to stop this TU from generating code from it.

questions.prompt: `template class RingBuffer<Order>;` is written for a type where one member function would be ill-formed for `Order`, though nothing ever calls it. What happens?
options: It compiles: explicit instantiation obeys the same lazy per-member rule as implicit instantiation.
It compiles: members that are ill-formed for the given argument are silently dropped from the instantiation.
It fails, but only at link time, when the symbol for the never-emitted invalid member is requested.
It fails: an explicit instantiation definition instantiates every member, including the uncalled one.
questions.explanation: Explicit instantiation of a class template instantiates *all* its members, so the whole class body must be valid for that argument — the cure is to explicitly instantiate individual members instead of the class. The 'same lazy rule' option is the natural inference from §17.7 and is precisely where it breaks: laziness is a property of *implicit* instantiation, and asking for the class by name is the opposite of implicit.

questions.prompt: For `template <class T> typename T::type f(T);` and `template <class T> void g(T) { typename T::type x; }`, what happens when each is called with an `int`?
options: `f` is a substitution failure that removes the candidate; `g` is a hard error raised from the body.
Both are substitution failures, since SFINAE covers everything the compiler substitutes `T` into.
Both are hard errors, since `T::type` is invalid for `int` no matter where it appears.
`f` is a hard error because return types are instantiated first; `g` is a substitution failure.
questions.explanation: SFINAE applies only to the *immediate context* — the signature, return type, and template parameter defaults. `f`'s return type is in that context, so the candidate is quietly dropped; `g`'s body is not, so substitution there produces a diagnosable error. The 'both are substitution failures' option overgeneralizes the rule in the direction people naturally assume, and it is exactly why 'SFINAE-friendly' became a stated API property of things like `std::iterator_traits`.

questions.prompt: Two overloads are written as `template <class T, std::enable_if_t<C<T>, int> = 0> void f(T);` and `template <class T, std::enable_if_t<C<T>, int> = nullptr> void f(T);`. What is the result?
options: Two distinct overloads, since default template arguments form part of a template's signature.
Two distinct overloads, since the `enable_if` conditions are evaluated before overload resolution starts.
One signature declared twice — a redefinition error, since the default arguments do not distinguish them.
One signature, but the compiler keeps the first declaration and silently discards the second.
questions.explanation: Default template arguments are not part of the signature, so both declarations declare the same template and the second is a redefinition; the fix is to give the two overloads genuinely different *conditions*. The 'distinct because defaults are part of the signature' option is the appealing one — the declarations do look different in source — but the same reasoning would also make `void h(int = 0)` and `void h(int = 1)` distinct, which nobody expects. (`= nullptr` here would not even typecheck against `int`.)

questions.prompt: In the `has_reserve` detection idiom, the partial specialization is matched on `std::void_t<decltype(std::declval<T&>().reserve(size_t{}))>`. What happens for a `T` with no `reserve`?
options: Substitution into the specialization's argument fails, so the specialization drops out and the `false_type` primary is chosen.
Substitution fails and that is a hard error, since a partial specialization is not a function and SFINAE does not apply.
The specialization still matches, because `void_t` discards its arguments without ever substituting into them.
The primary is chosen only when the second template argument is spelled out as `void` at the use site.
questions.explanation: The failure occurs in the immediate context of the partial specialization's argument list, so the specialization is simply not a match and the primary — inheriting `false_type` — is selected. The 'void_t discards its arguments' option is genuinely tempting because the alias really does throw them away, but CWG1558 settled that unused alias template arguments are still substituted; before that resolution, compilers that skipped the substitution broke this idiom and people needed a helper struct.

questions.prompt: Which description of a `requires`-expression's requirement kinds is correct?
options: A simple requirement `t.reserve(n);` checks that the call is valid and that its result type is `void`.
A nested requirement `requires C<T>;` checks that `C<T>` compiles, rather than that it is satisfied.
A compound requirement's `-> Concept` part is a documentation annotation with no checking effect.
A compound requirement `{ t.size() } noexcept -> std::convertible_to<size_t>;` checks validity, `noexcept`, and the result type.
questions.explanation: The compound form is the one that adds return-type and `noexcept` checking on top of validity, which is exactly what `void_t` detection could only do awkwardly. The 'simple requirement also checks for void' option is the near-miss: a simple requirement checks *only* that the expression is well-formed and says nothing about its type — checking the result is what the compound form is for. A nested requirement genuinely evaluates satisfaction, not mere validity.

questions.prompt: What does `void f(Arithmetic auto a, Arithmetic auto b);` declare?
options: A two-parameter template; each `auto` invents its own parameter, so `a` and `b` may have different types.
A one-parameter template; both `auto`s share one invented parameter, so `a` and `b` must have the same type.
Not a template at all — the parameters are deduced independently at each call, like `auto` variables.
An ill-formed declaration, unless both parameters are constrained by two distinct named concepts.
questions.explanation: Each `auto` parameter in the abbreviated form invents a fresh template parameter, so this is a two-parameter template and `f(1, 2.0)` is fine. The 'shared parameter' option is the intuitive misreading — the two `auto`s look like one repeated placeholder — and it matters because it is precisely why `template <Arithmetic T> void f(T, T)` and the abbreviated form are *not* interchangeable. The declaration is a template, which is what makes the constraint meaningful at all.

questions.prompt: Which constraint form can name the function's own parameters in its condition?
options: The constrained-parameter form, `template <Arithmetic T> void f(T x);`.
The trailing requires-clause, written after the parameter list: `void f(T x) requires C<x>;`.
The leading requires-clause, written before the return type: `requires C<T> void f(T x);`.
The abbreviated form with a constrained placeholder: `void f(Arithmetic auto x);`.
questions.explanation: Only the trailing requires-clause appears after the parameter list, so it is the only form in which the parameters are already in scope; the other three are all written before the parameters exist. This matters whenever a constraint depends on more than the template parameters themselves. The leading requires-clause is the closest miss — it is otherwise fully equivalent in expressive power, differing only in placement.

questions.prompt: One overload is constrained `requires std::is_integral_v<T>` and another `requires std::is_integral_v<T> && std::is_signed_v<T>`. A call with `int` matches both. What happens?
options: The more constrained one wins: the conjunction textually contains the first clause, which is enough to subsume it.
The less constrained one wins: having fewer atomic constraints ranks higher in the partial ordering.
Ambiguous: type traits are runtime values, so the compiler cannot normalize them into atomic constraints at all.
Ambiguous: atomic constraints match only when they come from the same source expression, so neither subsumes.
questions.explanation: Normalization compares atomic constraints by *identity of source expression plus parameter mapping*; the `is_integral_v<T>` written in the second declaration is a different atom from the one in the first, so no subsumption relation exists and the call is ambiguous. The 'textually contains it' option is the intuitive and wrong model — subsumption does no logical reasoning about what atoms mean, and copy-pasting a clause creates a fresh atom. Factoring the shared part into a named concept and conjoining at the top level is the fix.

questions.prompt: You wrap `Integral<T> && Signed<T>` in a `constexpr bool` variable template and constrain with `requires MyPred<T>`. Why does subsumption against a plain `requires Integral<T>` overload stop working?
options: Normalization decomposes `&&` only at the top level of the constraint-expression; a `bool` variable template is one opaque atom.
Normalization refuses to expand variable templates, so the constraint is dropped from the ordering entirely.
Subsumption requires every atom to be a concept name, so a constraint naming a `bool` is ill-formed outright.
Subsumption compares the runtime values of constraints, so two constraints that are both true always subsume.
questions.explanation: Only `&&` and `||` appearing at the top level of the constraint-expression decompose into a conjunction or disjunction during normalization; anything buried inside a `bool` expression or inside a `requires`-expression is preserved whole as a single atom. That is the practical argument for defining named *concepts* — which do expand — rather than `constexpr bool` helpers. The 'constraint is dropped entirely' option confuses being opaque with being ignored: the constraint is still checked, it just has no subsumption relationships.

questions.prompt: For a pack `args`, what is the difference between `g(h(args)...)` and `g(h(args...))`?
options: Both call `h` once per element; the difference is only whether the results are comma-separated in `g`'s argument list.
The first calls `h` once per element and passes the results to `g`; the second passes the whole pack to one call of `h`.
The first passes the whole pack to one call of `h`; the second calls `h` once per element and passes the results on.
Both pass the entire pack to a single call of `h`; the ellipsis position only affects the evaluation order.
questions.explanation: The ellipsis expands the pattern it follows: `h(args)...` makes `h(args)` the pattern and repeats it per element, while `h(args...)` expands the pack inside `h`'s own argument list. This is the single most useful rule for reading variadic code, and the reversed option is the mistake people make when they read `...` as a suffix on the whole call. Note that neither form guarantees evaluation order — only a comma fold does that.

questions.prompt: `template <class... Ts> auto sum(Ts... v) { return (v + ...); }` — what happens for `sum()` with no arguments?
options: It returns `0`, because the compiler supplies the operator's identity element for arithmetic folds.
It returns `void`, because an empty unary fold yields `void()` whatever the operator is.
It is ill-formed: a unary fold over an empty pack is permitted only for `&&`, `||` and the comma operator.
It is ill-formed: an empty pack makes every fold expression ill-formed, including `&&` and `||`.
questions.explanation: The three empty-pack defaults are `&&` → `true`, `||` → `false`, and `,` → `void()`; every other operator needs the binary form with an explicit identity, so `(v + ... + 0)` is the safe way to write this. The 'compiler supplies the identity' option is the natural expectation and is wrong because the language has no notion of an identity element for arbitrary operators — including user-defined ones. The `void()` answer applies only to the comma fold.

questions.prompt: You need each element of a pack processed in order, appending to a serialization buffer. Which is correct, and why?
options: `(f(v), ...)`, because a comma fold sequences left to right, while a call's argument list has unspecified order.
`g(f(v)...)`, because a function call's arguments are sequenced left to right, while a fold's order is unspecified.
Either one, because pack expansion is defined to proceed in the order the pack was declared.
Neither, because the pre-C++17 `initializer_list` trick is the only expansion form with guaranteed sequencing.
questions.explanation: A comma fold has a sequence point between elements and guarantees left-to-right evaluation; a pack expanded into a function call's argument list does not, since argument evaluation order is unspecified. The reversed option is the exact bug that bites people who write `g(f(v)...)` for side effects. The `initializer_list` hack also sequenced correctly, but it was the pre-C++17 workaround, not the only option today.

questions.prompt: Why is `std::forward(x)` — with the template argument omitted — a compile error?
options: It is well-formed and equivalent to `std::move`, since a named parameter is always an lvalue.
It is well-formed but a no-op, since a deduced `T` yields an lvalue reference in every case.
It is ill-formed only in C++11; since C++14 the argument may be deduced from the parameter.
It is ill-formed by design: `T` must be explicit, since deducing it from a named lvalue would lose the value category.
questions.explanation: `std::forward` is a conditional `static_cast<T&&>`, and the information it needs — how the *caller* passed the argument — lives in `T`, not in the named parameter, which is always an lvalue. Deducing `T` from `x` would therefore always produce an lvalue reference, silently defeating the purpose, so the signature is written to make deduction impossible. The 'well-formed but a no-op' option correctly predicts the behaviour deduction would give, but the library deliberately rejects it rather than letting it compile.

questions.prompt: Which argument cannot be passed through `template <class... A> void wrap(A&&... a) { target(std::forward<A>(a)...); }`?
options: A braced-init-list such as `{1, 2}`, because it has no type and is a non-deduced context.
A `const std::string&` lvalue, because deduction strips the const before reference collapsing runs.
A `std::unique_ptr` rvalue, because a move-only type cannot bind to a forwarding reference.
A `nullptr` literal, because `std::nullptr_t` is not among the deducible template argument types.
questions.explanation: A braced-init-list has no type, so it is a non-deduced context and `A` cannot be solved for — you must declare an `initializer_list` parameter or build the object at the call site. The `const std::string&` option is the plausible-sounding one: const is dropped for *by-value* parameters, but a forwarding reference preserves it, deducing `A = const std::string&`. Move-only types and `nullptr` forward without any trouble; the genuine failures alongside braced lists are `0`/`NULL`, bitfields, and overloaded function names.

questions.prompt: `advance_impl` is overloaded on `std::random_access_iterator_tag` and `std::input_iterator_tag`. Which is selected when the tag is `std::bidirectional_iterator_tag`?
options: The random-access overload, since tag hierarchies rank from the most capable category downwards.
The input overload, reached by a derived-to-base conversion, since no exact match is available.
Neither — the call is ambiguous, since the tag converts equally well to both declared tag types.
Neither — it fails to compile, since tag dispatch needs an overload for every category in the hierarchy.
questions.explanation: The tags form an inheritance chain in which `random_access` derives from `bidirectional` derives from `forward` derives from `input`, so a bidirectional tag converts to `input_iterator_tag` but *not* to `random_access_iterator_tag`. That one-directional conversion is what gives tag dispatch its automatic fallback ordering. The 'ambiguous' option assumes conversions run both ways along the hierarchy, which would defeat the whole design of `std::advance`.

questions.prompt: An `if constexpr` whose untaken branch contains code invalid for the current types is written inside a plain, non-template function. What happens?
options: The untaken branch is discarded exactly as inside a template — that is the point of the feature.
Both branches are discarded from codegen but still instantiated, so invalid code is tolerated either way.
The construct is ill-formed outright: `if constexpr` may only appear inside a template body.
Both branches are fully checked, because discarding statements happens only inside a template.
questions.explanation: Discarded-statement semantics apply only within a templated entity; in an ordinary function `if constexpr` merely prunes code generation and both branches are still fully type-checked. This surprises people trying to guard platform-specific code in a plain function. `if constexpr` is legal outside templates, so the ill-formed option is wrong — it just does much less than expected there.

questions.prompt: Why is `if constexpr (std::is_constant_evaluated())` a bug?
options: The branch is never taken, because `is_constant_evaluated` reports `false` in an `if constexpr` condition.
The branch is always taken: the condition is itself evaluated in a constant context, so it is always `true`.
The branch is taken only during constant evaluation, which is exactly what the idiom means to express.
It is ill-formed, because `is_constant_evaluated()` is not a constant expression and cannot appear there.
questions.explanation: An `if constexpr` condition must be a constant expression, so evaluating `std::is_constant_evaluated()` there is by definition a constant evaluation and it always yields `true` — the runtime branch is silently discarded. Use a plain `if (std::is_constant_evaluated())` or, in C++23, `if consteval`. The 'does what it says' option is the whole trap: the code reads as if it distinguishes the two contexts while unconditionally choosing one.

questions.prompt: How does `std::conditional_t<B, T, F>` differ from an `if constexpr` with the same condition?
options: Neither arm of `conditional_t` need be a valid type, since only the selected one is ever instantiated.
Only the selected arm of `conditional_t` is checked, while both `if constexpr` branches are always checked.
Both arms of `conditional_t` must name valid types, whereas a discarded `if constexpr` branch need not be valid code.
Both arms of `conditional_t` and both branches of `if constexpr` are fully checked in every context.
questions.explanation: `conditional_t` is an ordinary alias whose arguments are both written out and must both be well-formed types; `if constexpr` discards the untaken branch at instantiation, so that branch may contain code that would be ill-formed for the current arguments. The 'only the selected arm is checked' option imports the `if constexpr` rule into a context that has no such lazy behaviour — the arms are template arguments, and template arguments are always substituted.

questions.prompt: In an expression-template library, why is `auto e = a + b;` the number-one bug?
options: Nodes hold their operands by value, so `auto` is safe; the real hazard is only the huge type name in diagnostics.
`auto` deduces the evaluated element type, so the expression is computed eagerly and the loop fusion is lost.
Nodes extend the lifetime of any temporary operand through reference binding, leaving aliasing as the only hazard.
Nodes hold references to their operands, so a tree built from temporaries and stored in `auto` refers to destroyed objects.
questions.explanation: Expression nodes store references precisely so that no copies or allocations occur, which means the tree is only valid while its operands live; the design assumes immediate consumption by an assignment. The 'lifetime extension' option is the tempting near-miss — binding a temporary to a const reference does extend its lifetime, but only for a reference *variable* at the binding site, never through a reference member of a returned node. `auto` also does not force evaluation; it faithfully captures the node type.

questions.prompt: What is the thin-template/fat-base idiom for controlling code bloat?
options: Put type-independent logic in a non-template base so many instantiations share one body, as MSVC does for `vector<T*>`.
Mark every template `inline` so the linker can fold the duplicate COMDAT bodies down to a single copy.
Move templates out of headers and rely on implicit instantiation at link time to yield one shared body.
Replace class templates with macros, which the preprocessor expands exactly once per translation unit.
questions.explanation: The template becomes a thin, type-safe façade over an implementation that does not depend on `T` — which is how every `vector<T*>` instantiation can collapse onto one `vector<void*>` body. The `inline`-plus-folding option describes something real but unrelated: the linker already folds *identical* instantiations, and marking templates inline does nothing to make bodies for different `T` identical. Implicit instantiation never happens at link time.
